lead: The product of inertia measures how lopsided a flat area is about a pair of perpendicular axes. For a small element of area dA at coordinates (x, y), the contribution is xy dA; adding over the area gives Ixy = ∫xy dA. Unlike Ix and Iy, Ixy can be positive, negative, or zero. For every flat area there is a pair of principal axes about which Ixy vanishes and the second moments reach their largest and smallest values. Engineers use these axes to find the strong and weak bending directions of an unsymmetrical beam or a rolled section.
prereq: You need: 4.4 for Ix and Iy, and 4.5 for shifting a second moment.

sections.h3: Product of inertia and its sign

blocks.text: Take two perpendicular axes x and y in the plane of a flat area. Let dA be a small element at coordinates (x, y), measured in mm. Its product of inertia about the pair is xy dA. The product for the whole area is:

blocks.where: Ixy is the product of inertia about the x and y axes, in mm⁴; x and y are signed distances in mm from the two axes to the element dA.

blocks.text: Ix and Iy are always positive, but Ixy carries a sign. Elements in quadrants I and III give positive xy; elements in quadrants II and IV give negative xy. The net sign tells which way the area leans. If either axis is an axis of symmetry, each element has a mirror partner with the opposite x or y, so Ixy = 0. If one axis is a principal axis, Ixy = 0 by definition.
For axes moved parallel to the centroidal pair, the shift is:

blocks.where: Īxy is the centroidal product of inertia; A is the area in mm²; x̄ and ȳ are the signed distances in mm from the centroid to the new origin.

blocks.text: For a composite area, use I<sub>xy</sub> = Σ(Ī<sub>xy,i</sub> + A<sub>i</sub> x̄<sub>i</sub> ȳ<sub>i</sub>), summed over all parts about the same reference axes. Here Ī<sub>xy,i</sub> is the centroidal product of part i, A<sub>i</sub> its area, and x̄<sub>i</sub>, ȳ<sub>i</sub> its centroid coordinates from those axes. Keep the signs.

sections.h3: Rotation, principal axes, and Mohr's circle

blocks.text: Rotate the axes by θ counterclockwise from x to x′. The three quantities change as:
Ix′ = (Ix + Iy)/2 + ((Ix − Iy)/2) cos 2θ − Ixy sin 2θ ; Iy′ = (Ix + Iy)/2 − ((Ix − Iy)/2) cos 2θ + Ixy sin 2θ ; Ix′y′ = ((Ix − Iy)/2) sin 2θ + Ixy cos 2θ
blocks.where: θ is the angle from the old x-axis to the new x-axis, positive counterclockwise; Ix, Iy and Ixy are about the old axes.

blocks.text: At a principal axis, Ix′y′ = 0. Setting the product formula to zero gives the angle:

blocks.where: θp is the angle from the x-axis to a principal axis; the two roots differ by 90°, so the principal axes are perpendicular.
I₁ is the larger principal moment and I₂ the smaller; the square root is the radius R of the Mohr circle.

blocks.text: The sum is constant: I₁ + I₂ = Ix + Iy. Mohr's circle for inertia plots I horizontally and Ixy vertically, with Ixy positive upward. Its centre is C = (Ix + Iy)/2 and its radius is R = √(((Ix − Iy)/2)² + Ixy²). The circle cuts the horizontal axis at I₁ and I₂. The angle on the circle is 2θp, measured counterclockwise from the x-axis point (Ix, Ixy) to the principal point, the same sense as a counterclockwise turn of the axes. A few courses go on to the full three-dimensional inertia tensor; for a flat area, two second moments and one product are enough.
Use this order in an exam.

items: Sketch the area and mark the centroidal x and y axes.
Get Ix and Iy from 4.4 or a standard table.
Compute Īxy with its sign. If the axes are not centroidal, shift with Ixy = Īxy + A x̄ ȳ.
Compute C = (Ix + Iy)/2 and R = √(((Ix − Iy)/2)² + Ixy²).
Write I₁ = C + R and I₂ = C − R.
Find θp from tan 2θp = −2Ixy/(Ix − Iy). Check the root by putting θ into Ix′; it must equal I₁ or I₂.
Draw the principal axes and label the larger moment. The other principal axis is 90° away.

figure.caption: The flow takes the triangle's Ix, Iy and Ixy into a Mohr circle, then reads I₁, I₂ and θp. Notice that the centre is the average of Ix and Iy, and the radius sets both principal moments.

spec.title: Finding principal axes for the triangle
spec.aria: A downward flow takes Ix, Iy and Ixy into a Mohr circle with centre 877500, radius 527192, principal moments 1404692 and 350308, and angle 25.1 degrees.

examples.question: A right-angled triangle has base b = 60 mm along the x-axis and height h = 90 mm along the y-axis. The right angle is at the origin. Find Ix, Iy and Ixy about centroidal axes parallel to the legs. Then find the principal moments and the angle of the principal axes from the x-axis.
steps: Area A = (1/2) × 60 × 90 = 2700 mm². The centroid is at x̄ = 20 mm and ȳ = 30 mm from the legs.
Ix about the centroidal axis parallel to the base: Ix = b h³/36 = 60 × 729000 / 36 = 1,215,000 mm⁴.
Iy about the centroidal axis parallel to the height: Iy = h b³/36 = 90 × 216000 / 36 = 540,000 mm⁴.
Ixy about the centroidal axes: Ixy = −b²h²/72 = −(3600 × 8100)/72 = −405,000 mm⁴. The negative sign comes from the area lying mostly in quadrants II and IV about the centroidal pair.
Angle: tan 2θp = −2Ixy/(Ix − Iy) = −2(−405000)/675000 = 1.2. So 2θp = 50.2° and θp = 25.1° from the x-axis. Substitution into Ix′ gives I₁, so the larger principal moment is at 25.1°.
examples.answer: Ix = 1,215,000 mm⁴, Iy = 540,000 mm⁴, Ixy = −405,000 mm⁴; the principal moments are I₁ = 1,404,692 mm⁴ and I₂ = 350,308 mm⁴, with the larger moment at θp = 25.1° from the x-axis.
examples.check:
import math
b = 60.0
h = 90.0
Ix = b*h**3/36
Iy = h*b**3/36
Ixy = -(b*b*h*h)/72
C = (Ix + Iy)/2
R = math.hypot((Ix - Iy)/2, Ixy)
I1 = C + R
I2 = C - R
theta = 0.5*math.degrees(math.atan2(-2*Ixy, Ix - Iy))
print(round(Ix))
print(round(Iy))
print(round(Ixy))
print(round(C))
print(round(R))
print(round(I1))
print(round(I2))
print(round(theta, 1))

traps: Losing the sign of Ixy: a negative product rotates the principal axis the other way from a positive one of the same magnitude.

Mixing quantities taken about different axes — for example Ix and Iy about the centroidal pair but Ixy about the legs. All three must be about the same pair. If the question asks for principal centroidal axes, shift Ixy with Ixy = Īxy + A x̄ ȳ first.
Reporting 2θp as θp; the formula gives twice the angle. The two values of 2θp differ by 180°, so the two principal directions θp differ by 90°.
Assuming every centroidal pair is principal; Ixy is zero only for a symmetry pair or a principal pair.
Writing units of Ixy as mm² or kg m²; for an area it is mm⁴, while a mass product of inertia uses kg m².

quiz.q: Define the product of inertia of a plane area about the x and y axes, with its unit.
quiz.a: Ixy = ∫xy dA, where x and y are signed coordinates of element dA; unit mm⁴.

quiz.q: Why is Ixy zero when the y-axis is an axis of symmetry?
quiz.a: Each element at (x, y) has a mirror partner at (−x, y). The products xy and −xy cancel in pairs, so the integral is zero.

quiz.q: For an area, Ix = 8.0 × 10⁶ mm⁴, Iy = 4.0 × 10⁶ mm⁴, Ixy = 3.0 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Find I₁ and I₂.
A non-square rectangle has centroidal axes x, y tilted at 30° to its sides. Is Ixy zero? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The sides are symmetry axes, so Ixy is zero only when x or y is along a side. A 30° tilted pair gives a nonzero product because the mirror cancellation no longer works about both axes.

quiz.q: Write the formula for the angle of the principal axes.
quiz.a: tan 2θp = −2Ixy/(Ix − Iy), where θp is measured from the x-axis.

quiz.q: On Mohr's circle for inertia, why is Ixy plotted positive upward?
quiz.a: With Ixy positive upward, the point (Ix′, Ix′y′) moves counterclockwise by 2θ when the axes turn counterclockwise by θ. The angle 2θp is read counterclockwise on the circle in the same sense as the physical rotation. The centre, radius and principal values do not depend on the plotting choice.

quiz.q: For Ix = Iy = 10 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and Ixy = 4 × 10⁶ mm⁴, find the principal moments and θp.
quiz.a: C = (10 + 10)/2 × 10⁶ = 10 × 10⁶ mm⁴, R = √(0² + 4²) × 10⁶ = 4 × 10⁶ mm⁴. I₁ = 14 × 10⁶ mm⁴, I₂ = 6 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Since Ix − Iy = 0, the tan formula has zero denominator; 2θp = −90° gives I₁, so θp = −45° (45° clockwise from x). Check: Ix′ = (10 − 4 sin(−90°)) × 10⁶ = 14 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The other principal axis is θp = +45° and gives I₂.

beyond: Not for the exam. A few courses write the three-dimensional inertia tensor as a 3×3 matrix; its eigenvalues are the principal moments and its eigenvectors the principal axes. This chapter stays flat, so two second moments and one product are enough. In machine design, the same rotation formulas pick the strong axis of an unsymmetrical beam or a pressed-steel channel. Search 'Mohr's circle for area moments of inertia' and 'principal centroidal axes'.
